transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-19 15:00 PST
Duration: ~75 mins
Attendees: Maya, Jordan, Evan, Sasha, Tessa, Ben, Ravi, Claire
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai (auto)

Auto-generated summary: internal enablement, roleplay and demo script practice (may be incomplete)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay team, welcome — this is the enablement sim lab, we're going to run two short roleplays and then a demo script drill. goal is quick, actionable takeaways. um, Jordan you good to kick off with messaging framing?

[00:18] Jordan Patel: Yeah, I'm good. Quick framing — remember our elevator: "Redwood is inference-first: predictable latency, cost controls, and unified runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments." Keep it punchy. Not "model management" — it's about serving the model in production.

[00:42] Tessa Moore: Quick Q — saying "inference-first" to customers, do we need to define that? sometimes they hear 'inference' as just API hosting.

[00:55] Jordan Patel: Good point. Add a one-liner: "Inference-first means we optimize for production economics — latency, throughput, and reliability — not just model access." (note: sometimes transcriber shows 'production economics' as 'product economics')

[01:15] Ben Hall: Can we also flag 'cost controls' like batching and KV cash. (laugh) 'K-V cash' is a new one.

[01:27] Jordan Patel: Haha yes, KV cache — auto-prefix caching — highlight it's transparent to devs. That helps with token cost without changing prompts.

[01:40] Roleplay round 1 (AE opens)
[01:42] Sasha Kim (role: AE): Hey Alex thanks for taking a minute. Quick background — we help engineering teams ship LLM features with predictable latency and lower unit cost. Can I ask — are you currently hosting models in the cloud, dedicated infra, or doing any private deployment?

[01:58] (short pause, simulated customer)
[02:05] Tessa Moore (role: customer): We're on BigCloud managed endpoints but hitting unpredictable p99 latency spikes and billing surprises.

[02:13] Sasha Kim: Thanks. That's pretty common — can you share what's most painful? Is it burstiness, slow warm-up, or procurement constraints?

[02:24] Tessa Moore: It's a combo — bursts and then sudden cost jumps, and our security team wants keys in a KMS not in third-party logs.

[02:33] Sasha Kim: Great. Quick response: Redwood offers dedicated capacity for predictable throughput and a private VPC option so keys stay in your KMS/HSM. We also have smart routing and automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if capacity constrained — so you avoid surprises.

[02:50] Jordan Patel: Call out the SLA-backed latency targets for dedicated, and that we surface token-level cost breakdowns in Console — that's a seller-friendly detail.

[03:05] Ben Hall: Objection practice — customer says "sounds expensive". How to respond?

[03:12] Maya Chen: Two-part answer: 1) show the unit economics: batching, caching, and quantization recommendations typically reduce per-token cost by X-30%xx (note: speaker mumbles actual percent) 2) point to rollout strategy — start hosted for quick dev, then shift heavy throughput to dedicated when predictable.

[03:35] Roleplay round 2 (SE enters)
[03:38] Evan Rivera (role: SE): Hi — if you want to run a throughput test, we can compile a benchmark showing latency and p99 under your sequence length distribution. We can also show compatibility with your internal KMS.

[03:50] Tessa Moore: And what about model parity vs what BigCloud offers?

[03:56] Evan Rivera: We curate open models and provide Redwood-verified profiles; if an equivalent BigCloud model is available, we can run side-by-side to show latency and cost — often our kernel selection and batching gives better cost at similar latency. Also smart routing can fallback to cheaper variants if there's capacity pressure.

[04:20] Claire Nguyen: There's often a hiccup on explaining 'smart routing' — customers ask "does my traffic leave region?" How to reassure?

[04:28] Jordan Patel: Clarify policy-based routing: we route according to your rules — region, latency SLO, cost tier — and for private deployments traffic stays within your VPC as configured. 

[04:42] Demo script drill intro
[04:44] Maya Chen: Okay demo script — we're going to run a 3-min opener and a 7-min focused walkthrough. Evan you'll demo latency/throughput scenario, then Jordan you'll show a canary rollout policy in Console. Sasha you'll close the narrative. Ready?

[05:01] Evan Rivera: Starting clip: show runbook first — open console, pull model catalog, show model variant selector, then run a small live query, point out streaming tokens and token-level cost breakdown. (inaudible keyboard)

[05:25] [Screen share note: demo artifacts referenced - quick-deck-link, bench-spreadsheet, security-pack.pdf]

[05:40] Evan Rivera: Live query: "Hello, summarize this meeting" — show streaming, show latency 40ms on small prompt, then change prompt size to 2k tokens and show p95 jump.

[06:10] Tessa Moore: In the roleplay, the customer will interrupt and ask 'why not use BigCloud for everything?'

[06:18] Jordan Patel: Terse competitive line: "BigCloud focuses on model access and infra; Redwood focuses on inference economics and observability — we give you the knobs so you can control latency, cost, and compliance without rebuilding the stack."

[06:35] Ben Hall: Call-out: mention audit logs + SOC2 and SAML SSO when the conversation is about compliance.

[06:46] Sasha Kim: Quick objection: 'We can't move data to third party.' Response?

[06:52] Maya Chen: We have a private control plane option with VPC and on-prem package; keys can stay on customer KMS / HSM. For some regulated customers we do an air-gapped deploy.

[07:10] Jordan Patel: Add the phrase: "customer-managed networking" — resonates with security folks.

[07:25] Roleplay — tough objection drill (customer: wants max throughput and absolute p99 under 50ms)

[07:30] Evan Rivera: Technical reply: We'll need to profile your sequence lengths and concurrency. Often it's a combination of larger instance types, optimized kernels, and reduced sequence lengths or caching. We can run a 72-hour bench to give data.

[07:50] Tessa Moore: If they ask about quantization quality loss?

[07:55] Jordan Patel: Be honest: quantization can reduce memory and cost; we give model and quantization recommendations by workload and run quality monitoring tied to prompt sets so we can detect regressions. Offer a small eval run.

[08:10] Breakout micro-practice (each trainee records a 45–90s rebuttal)
[08:15] [background chatter: record, hey that's good, cut, retake]

[09:05] Sasha Kim (playback): I tried a short opener and my 'why Redwood' felt too long. Please critique.

[09:12] Maya Chen: Trim to two sentences: 1) value prop, 2) 1 concrete example/pain point, 3) ask a qualifying question. Example: "We help engineers ship LLM features with predictable latency and control over per-token costs. Last week we helped a team reduce their inference unit cost by switching to batch-aware routing — are you tracking per-route token costs today?"

[09:42] Ben Hall: That last line is strong — turns into a discovery question.

[09:50] Competitive nuance: ModelServeX talking points
[09:52] Jordan Patel: ModelServeX sells prepackaged endpoints with tight integration to their cloud — good for quick lift-and-shift. But downsides: limited observability into token-level cost and less flexible private deployment options. Use comparatives: "If you need vendor-locked endpoints with minimal ops, go theirs. If you need control and predictable economics, choose us."

[10:20] Tessa Moore: Be careful with tone — say "they focus on X" not attack.

[10:34] OnPremCo mention: several customers still choose them for air-gapped needs but they lack modern batching and often have higher unit cost.

[10:48] Demo painpoint handling: live warm-up issues
[10:50] Evan Rivera: Show warm-up plan: prefix caching + warm-up traffic + autoscaling policies and how we can pre-warm specific routes.

[11:08] Claire Nguyen: Quick ask — can we add a short slide for common procurement questions?

[11:15] Maya Chen: Yes, include procurement play: trial credits, pilot duration, basic T&Cs, and a contact for legal.

[11:30] Objection: 'I need private deployment but no devops team'

[11:35] Jordan Patel: We offer a private control plane that's managed, or an on-prem package with partner integrators. Emphasize partner program + professional services.

[11:52] Mid-meeting recap (Maya): Quick hits — tighten opener, record 2 demo clips (latency and rollout), update one-pager with procurement bullets, bench tests schedule.

[12:10] Playbook update discussion
[12:12] Ravi Desai: Should we add a short matrix: "When to recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private"?

[12:20] Jordan Patel: Yes: Hosted = fast POC, Dedicated = predictable throughput & SLA, Private = regulated + data residency. Add cost/ops footnote.

[12:40] Short lightning roleplay — speed round objections
[12:42] (rapid back-and-forth, timestamps condensed)
[13:05] Sasha Kim: "We're concerned about vendor lock-in" — quick answer?

[13:12] Evan Rivera: "We support model version pinning and exportable configs; we also recommend hybrid strategies to avoid lock-in."

[13:28] Ben Hall: "Can you show me token-level billing?"

[13:32] Jordan Patel: "Yes, Console has token-level breakdowns by route and model; we'll share a screenshot."

[13:46] Demo: Canary rollout in Console (Jordan)
[13:48] Jordan Patel: Walkthrough: routes -> create rollout -> set canary 5% -> automatic fallback to cheaper variant -> show trace & alerting hooks. Mention there are tracing hooks for error analysis.

[14:30] Technical deep-dive question from Ben: How do kernels choose at runtime?

[14:35] Evan Rivera: Runtime selects optimized kernels based on model architecture and sequence length distribution — it can choose quantized-friendly paths when appropriate.

[14:50] Crosstalk and short interruptions (recording error noted)
[15:05] Audience ask: "What stories resonate most with procurement?"

[15:10] Maya Chen: Procurement likes predictable costs, proof of integration with KMS, and clear SLAs. Always have the security pack and basic SOW ready.

[15:26] Competitive nuance: BigCloud AI Endpoints pricing model
[15:30] Jordan Patel: BigCloud often charges per-inference compute plus egress in a way that surprises teams. Our message: transparent per-token with tooling to attribute costs to product routes.

[15:50] Practice clip review — play one recorded rebuttal (Sasha)
[15:52] Sasha Kim (recording): "We help engineering teams move fast without unpredictable bills; can you tell me where you see budget leakage today?" (slight stutter at end)

[16:10] Feedback: tighten second clause to be more specific, use an example.

[16:30] Logistics: who uploads clips to playbook?

[16:32] Maya Chen: Jordan will collect and upload to playbook repo. Evan will add timestamps and short meta notes.

[16:45] Bench lab scheduling discussion
[16:47] Ravi Desai: We need customer sequence distributions and sample prompts to mimic production. Create a template for bench requests.

[16:58] Claire Nguyen: I'll draft the bench request template.

[17:05] Quick Q: anyone mention 'edge compute' in objections?

[17:09] Ben Hall: Yes some customers want edge inference; we can say we support regional routing and partner to edge devices, but it's not our core focus.

[17:22] Final roleplay: AE closes for pilot
[17:24] Sasha Kim (AE): "Would you be open to a 4-week pilot — we run a bench, provide a private test project, and share results?"

[17:32] Tessa Moore: Yes that sounds fine, need legal and budget confirmation.

[17:36] Maya Chen: Good — record that as a follow-up for bench scheduling and security doc share.

[17:50] Quick meta: clip length advice
[17:52] Jordan Patel: Keep clips between 45–90 seconds, one nugget per clip — opener, cost rebuttal, compliance reassurance.

[18:05] Closing recap (Maya): Action items and owners — we already listed. Any final comments?

[18:12] Ben Hall: Please ensure the one-pager has the procurement bullets.

[18:18] Tessa Moore: Can we get a template email to request bench time?

[18:22] Maya Chen: Yes we'll add a bench-request email template to the assets.

[18:30] End of main session — people stay on for two quick pairing recordings (off transcript)

[75:00] Meeting ended

Notes on transcription quality: some speaker labels and numbers may be off; there are a few garbled percent numbers and a misspelling 'KV cash' for KV cache in a couple places. Recordings and uploaded clips will be the source-of-truth.
